questions.q: What fundamentally distinguishes a scatter plot's shelf setup from a bar, line, or pie chart in this chapter?
options: A scatter plot plots two measures against each other, instead of a dimension against a measure
A scatter plot cannot use the Sample Superstore dataset
A scatter plot requires exactly three dimensions
A scatter plot is the only chart type that uses the Marks card
questions.explain: Every other chart in this chapter plots a measure against a category (dimension); a scatter plot instead treats both axes as numeric, plotting one measure against another.

questions.q: What happens if you put a measure on Columns and a measure on Rows with no dimension anywhere in the view?
options: Tableau aggregates both measures as a sum and plots exactly one mark — the grand totals against each other
Tableau throws an error and refuses to render the view
Tableau automatically adds a trend line
Tableau defaults to a bar chart instead of a scatter plot
questions.explain: With no dimension to break the aggregation apart, both measures collapse into their grand totals, producing a single plotted point.

questions.q: What does dragging a dimension onto Detail on the Marks card do in a scatter plot?
options: It splits the single aggregated mark into one mark per member of that dimension, without changing color
It removes the dimension from the view entirely
It automatically colors each mark a different color
It converts the scatter plot into a treemap
questions.explain: Detail splits an aggregated mark into multiple marks based on a dimension's members, distinct from Color, which does the same split but also assigns each member a distinct color.

questions.q: What does a trend line's R-squared value tell you?
options: How well the fitted line matches the actual plotted points
The exact future value the measure will reach next year
The total number of marks in the scatter plot
Whether the underlying data source is a live connection or an extract
questions.explain: R-squared measures how well a statistical model (like a linear trend line) fits the observed data — it's a goodness-of-fit statistic, not a forecast or a causal claim.

questions.q: When is a scatter plot the wrong chart choice, according to this lesson?
options: When the real question is about category comparison or change over time, rather than the relationship between two measures
Whenever the dataset contains more than 1,000 rows
Scatter plots are always the correct choice regardless of the question
Only when using a live SQL Server connection instead of an extract
questions.explain: If there's really only one measure of interest and the question is about categories or time, a bar or line chart puts that measure on an axis where it belongs — a scatter plot is built specifically for relationships between two measures.
